speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ELECTION OF MR. WILLIAM DUFF QUEF.NS-LUNENBURG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be
permitted to join my congratulations to those of other hon. members upon Your Honour's re-election as Speaker of this House, a choice-which was received1, as was to have been expected, with' most gratifying unanimity.
As Your Honour is aware, rule 13 of the House provides that at the commencement of every parliament, as soon as an Address has been agreed to in answer tc His Excellency's Speech, a chairman of committees of the House shall ibe elected who Shall serve as Deputy Speaker. I have no doubt that after a continuous, and-may I add?- exemplary, uninterrupted occupancy of the Speaker's chair for a period of seven weeks, during which time the debate on the Address has been carried on, Your Honour will look not without favour upon the exercise by the House of the power given it under this rule.
I hope that the name I am about, to propose as that of chairman of committees may also be cordially received by bon. members in all parts of the House.

Supply-Customs
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) h'as had an experience in this House of some nine years. As hon. members who sat with him in the last and the preceding 'parliaments will know, he possesses the many qualifications which eminently fit him to serve in the important capacity of Chairman of Committees and Deputy Speaker. In the discharge of the important duties of this joint office he will bring a knowledge of the rules acquired1 by dareful observation and study and in no small measure by practical experience; he will bring not less a disposition to foe fearless and impartial in the exercise of an authority which in its character is essentially judicial.
I have therefore great pleasure in moving, seconded- by Mr. Lapointe,
That William Duff, Esquire, member for the electoral district of Queens-Lunenbitrg, be appointed chairman of the committees of the whole House.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. GEORGE H. BOIVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise): Mr. Chairman, while the entire estimate for the outside service of the Department of Customs and Excise is included in vote 349, amounting to $10,884;,390, I think it would be better, if the committee would agree, to take up the different items separately, discuss them as they are reached, and after each separate item has been approved, have one formal vote adopting the whole resolution. I really do not understand why it has always been the custom to have all the items of the Department of Customs and Excise estimates embodied in one vote, but we have followed the usual custom this year making it much easier to make comparisons with the items required in previous years.
Before going into the details I desire to say that it is not through any spirit of bravado that I happen to be the first minister to present his estimates. I at once ask the committee to grant me thq indulgence which is usually given to a new minister submitting his estimates to the House for the first time. That does not mean, however, that I am not prepared with the aid of my officers to give to the members all possible information, and if there is any information that I do not have available at the moment, the members of the committee may rest assured that I will do my best to get it for them. If they insist on the information, there will be no attempt on my part to press the item until such information has been brought down. It is true that an inquiry into the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise is being carried on and there is a rule of the House that provides that matters pertaining to a committee cannot be discussed in the House until that committee has made its final report. I think, [DOT] however, it will be possible for hon. members to ask such questions and for me to give such answers in connection with the estimates as will give this committee all the information required, without in any way referring to what is going on at present before the customs investigating committee. The only information, perhaps, that I cannot give definitely will be concerning the organization of the preventive service staff of the Department of Customs and Excise. I want to say very frankly to the committee that the preventive service staff, organized under the vote of $350,000 which was included in the supplementary estimates of last year, has not been entirely satisfactory. Hon. members will ascertain that only about $35,000, or one-
Supply-Customs

tenth of the amount voted, has been expended. I thought it better to spend little than to expend a very large amount and get no results. I am asking for a re-vote of the same amount this year, with the intention of expending it in the same careful and cautious manner, and if it is impossible for me to describe exactly the plans I have under consideration for the reinforcement of that staff, it is because I desire to await the outcome of the customs inquiry and to follow in so far as it may be possible the suggestions which may be made by that committee. I am sure that the work of the committee will not be wasted effort, and that the suggestions received from the committee both as to possible amendments to the Customs Act and as to the reorganization of the preventive service staff will be enlightening, and that it will be possible for us to adopt them in many respects. With these few preliminary remarks, and asking once more for the indulgence of hon. members I would suggest that we proceed, Mr. Chairman, to consider the item you have just read.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of
the House that the resolution be considered item by item?

I take it, Mr. Chairman, that we all agree with the minister that that is the only thing to do. We always have done it; sometimes we do the right thing, and I think we had better continue to do so. Just at the commencement and before discussing this item I would like my hon. friend to give me all the information he can in connection with the salaries. The first item is, I suppose, the one we will take up, amounting to $6,723,815, and it deals with the salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion, including pay for overtime of officers and so on. I notice there is an increase in that particular item. I would like the minister to give the House some information as to how he finds these services, and if there are any changes which he desires to make, as well as his observations on the reference there made to the Civil Service Act, in connection with employees.

The words "notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act" do not apply in any sense to the appointment of the employees. The salaries paid out of this item of $6,723,815, which shows an increase over last year of $271,447.61 are paid to civil servants in the outside service but all appointed by the Civil Service Commission. The words "notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act" refer only to pay for over-

>
[DOT]
time. The officers for overtime work are chosen by the department and the overtime salary is paid without reference to the Civil Service Act. The overtime rate is 50 cents per hour on week days and 60 cents per hour on Sunday. The Sunday and much overtime labour of customs officers is repaid by the railway or steamboat companies that take advantage of the services of these officers.
Do they pay the civil servants direct?

No. The officers are paid by us, and the company is billed by the department for the overtime. None of our officers are ever obliged to work overtime on Sunday but those who do so voluntarily and willingly are paid.
Additions to staff under this item account for the sum of $59,210, but that amount is offset by the decrease in salaries to promotions, retirements and appointments of senior officers whose positions are taken by new men or by men promoted from an inferior rank so that in reality the additions to staff mean an increase of $1,880. The statutory increases provided for by the Civil Service Act, with which all the old members of this House are quite familiar, account for the sum of $169,530.
Another increase in this item is for contingent expenses. They are increased by about $97,492.61. The major portion of that amount, about $60,000, is made up of overtime salaries and special salaries paid to watchmen for boats at Halifax, Windsor and other ports, but specially at Halifax, where all boats coming into the harbour laden with liquor must be placed under guard by the department, and the officers must be paid for watching the boats. While the amount, $97,000 may appear large, I should state at once that this amount like the overtime paid to our officers on Sundays, is reimbursed to the department by the owners of the boats and schooners requiring the services of these watchmen.

I take it from what my hon. friend says that he has some new regulations in connection with this particular branch of the department's work. He tells us that there is a substantial increase in this connection. I assume that must be because we have some change in the regulations. My hon. friend shakes his head. If there is no change in the regulations, why does the amount go up so much? Perhaps it would be more convenient if my hon. friend would give the committee just exactly how the item

Supply-Customs
is made up, so that we can see where the increases come in, and how the expenditure compares with last year.

The total salaries amount to 85,753,815, as compared with 85,579,000 last year; that is, the difference in total salaries is about 8175,000. As I stated before, the statutory increases account for 8169,530, and the additions to the staff, very few of which were made, are almost entirely compensated by the decrease in salaries paid to the new appointees.

Is it convenient at this point to give the additions to the
staff?

The net additions to staff are 48 men, receiving salaries amounting altogether to 850,210. The total number of officers paid is 3,583. The total amount paid in salaries is 85,753,815.
Mr. M,ANION: What were the 48 additions?

New officers were appointed at different ports where the work had become so heavy that the inspectors requested additions to the staff and a few new offices were
opened.
At what places?

A new office was opened at Malagash, near Amherst; there was an addition of one clerk and three typists to the Montreal office; another customs excise officer at Berthierville; an additional officer required for preventive work to take charge of office during the absence of the sub-collector at Quebec; a new outport was established at Cowansville, and a new officer appointed there; an additional officer for supervising the trans-shipment of goods at Beauceville; six customs excise examiners appointed at Bridge-burg; one at Fort William, one at Ingersoll, one at Whitby, seven additional officers at Windsor, one at Calgary, one at Lethbridge, one at Abbotsford, one at Nelson, British Columbia, a female examiner at New Westminster, and two additional men for the Pacific highway at New Westminster.
As I get it there are three new offices?
There are three new offices.

Just in connection with the matter of offices, I wonder if my hon. friend has considered the question
of the multiciplity of office. That is something that has a great deal to do with the very matter the committee is now considering, and that is the question of properly collecting our customs. I think it is pretty well notorious that the way to get goods in at valuations which do not jibe is to multiply the offices. I wonder if my hon. friend has ever considered whether it would not be a right thing to decrease the offices and adopt rather the standard of the United States in this regard where their offices are merely a fraction of ours, having regard to the activities carried on. Would it not be better to do that instead of further increasing offices, the only effect of which is to make it just that much more easy for importers to get their goods into this country at an improper valuation and on an improper basis?

I agree entirely with what
my hon. friend says. In fact I might perhaps give a list of some of the offices that we have already abolished. We have abolished more, offices than we have created.
Would my hon. friend give the names of those abolished?

There were three officers
employed at Baddeck. It was found that these officers stationed at that place could not perform their work effectively and the positions were discontinued.

Is the office at
Baddeck closed?

Yes, there is no one left
there now except possibly a preventive officer. At Barrington Passage the postion of customs excise examiner has been vacant since the appointment of Mr. Gray as collector. That position, instead of being filled, has been discontinued. The position of customs excise examiner at Bridgewater has been discontinued; the position of customs excise examiner at Digby has been discontinued. The officer stationed at Point Acone, North Sydney is no longer required there for the entering and clearing of vessels, and that office has been discontinued. Have any representations
been made to the minister with respect to the necessity for new officials on that part of the coast line of New Brunswick bordered by the gulf of St. Lawrence? So far as I know the department over which the minister has the honour to preside has not appointed a single new preventive officer in that locality and there is no prevention of the smuggling of liquor from those points. That matter is under consideration, and I am glad my hon. friend has brought it up. shores of the three Maritime provinces. I hope it will be possible for us to co-operate to a certain extent with the administrators of the provincial laws in an effort to put an end to rum-running and to protect not only the federal revenue but the revenue of the different provinces concerned. There has always been some difficulty in making arrangements with provincial governments for the protection of liquor revenue because the provincial governments making seizures have always claimed the right to sell the liquor and to retain the proceeds. This deprives the federal government of the duty or excise tax, as the case may be, on that liquor. We do not generally pay awards to our informers until the duty or excise tax, as the case may be, has been paid. For that reason the question is a difficult one to adjust. We have had conferences recently with Mr. Paton of Prince Edward Island who, if I remember correctly, is chairman of the Prohibition Commission there. We have had frequent conferences with the president of the Quebec Liquor Commission concerning the matter, and I hope very shortly to be able to devise some way which will be acceptable to the provinces and also to the department so that the officers of the two governments may work together in close harmony.

has been made is that in the three Maritime provinces-I think this applies equally to the three-not all the provincial officers, but a few of them, at the request of the mayors of their cities, or the provincial govern-4 p.m. ment, or the chairman of the prohibition commissions, or whatever organization is functioning, have applied to us for what is commonly called a writ of assistance. We have always insisted that this liquor shall pay customs or excise duty to the government exactly as my hon. friend has suggested, but the difficulty arises from the fact that the provincial governments claim that they pay the salaries of these men; that the proceeds of seizures made by these men all go to the federal treasury, and that the only advantage they get out of it is that they get their liquor for the price of the duty instead of having to pay the duty plus the cost which is very small. The late Minister of Customs and his predecessor went to Toronto and saw the actual conditions. A site was purchased from the city at about one-third of its value cfver twelve years ago. This lot was situated on the south side of Front street, and was bought in 1917 for $110,000. The hon. Minister of Customs stated a few moments ago that the appointment at Kingsville, Ontario was made by the Civil Service Commission. I desire to submit a letter in this connection under date of February 5. This is rather a complicated affair, and quite difficult to explain by letter.

I carried out instructions on appointment, and ou presentation of same was informed that my duties would not begin until authorization from Minister of the Department at Ottawa had arrived.
Through some reason, the news of my appointment became known, and our friends here became active, by wire, with the result that although I was appointed on June 30, headed the examination, served approximately three years in France, was rejected on account of a charge by some political henchmen ot this district, but the enclosed letters will explain all I think to your satisfaction.
This appointment did not follow the usual procedure, and instead of going through the commission, came from the department by wire, in due time being passed through the usual channels.

Telegraph Companies, whose agent I was here. These letters are from the inspectors who personally checked my office at the time I resigned.

You can easily see what becomes of the charges of the department, against the name of a man who had served his country in the time of need; charges that had not the slightest foundation, nothing more or less than a political dodge from beginning to end.
When we fellows enlisted they did not stop to ask what our politics were.
The defeated representative of South Essex, Mr. Graham, with whom I had several interviews, the first one the day that I had been informed that the appointment was made definitely. I immediately produced the result of my marks, also the appointment, and said:	"In view of the
facts already stated by you with these official documents in your hand, how do you account for another man receiving the appointment?"
Mr. Graham: "Well, the Customs Department have got busy, Mac."
Mr. McCallum:	"You have just finished telling me
that this could not possibly be done."
Mr. Graham:	"But of course, you understand this
is not my department?"
Mr. McCallum:	"This may not be in your department, but this is your constituency, and are you aware of the fact that there- are hundreds of returned soldiers in South Essex?"

The next interview I had with Mr. Graham was the day that he was endorsed as Liberal candidate in South Essex.

I should like to bring to
the attention of the minister a condition which exists at the head of the lakes. Perhaps it hardly fits in under this item, but it is just as appropriate under this item as under any other as far as I can see, so I do not think it is out of order, Mr. Chairman.
There is at the present time r.t the head of the lakes a bus line- running from Port Arthur to Duluth, a distance of something over 200 miles. That bus line has a passenger service each way daily, but for some reason, owing to a provision in the Customs Act- ' I do not know when it was -introduced- these busses cannot carry anybody on the Canadian side; that is, a man, woman or child cannot get on one of these busses at

Supply-Customs
the head of the lakes and get off before reaching the international boundary. If the bus permits such a thing to happen, it is apparently breaking a law which brings these busses under the same control as applies in the case of passenger and freight boats on the Great Lakes, which are not permitted to call from one Canadian port to another. Apparently the same law applies to the bus lines as applies to the steamship lines. I do not know of any reason in the world why that law should apply to bus lines, but such I believe is the case. The fact remains that a man, woman or child living in Fort William or Port Arthur, or a farmer out in the country, cannot get on one of these busses and go for any distance less than the 55 miles to the international boundary. If anyone wishes to make a shorter trip, he must hire a special car, if 'he has not a car of his own. It certainly seems a ridiculous proposition that these busses should be running to and fro daily and yet the farmers in the neighbourhood1 'and the citizens of Fort William and Port Arthur who have not automobiles of their own should not, be permitted to use these busses and travel any distancs they wish, twenty-five or thirty or forty miles without the bus breaking the law. I remember laying this matter before the then Minister of Customs last year or possibly two years ago. I have also written recently to the present 'Minister of Customs, but he has not had time to deal with the matter. Certainly it would appear to me to be reasonable to permit these busses to handle Canadian traffic at 'least until a Canadian bus line is established. The present bus lines are managed by American companies, and until such time as there is a Canadian bus line competing-and I would certainly favour a Canadian line-it would appear to me that the present restrictions should be wiped out and the people allowed to take advantage of these busses travelling to and fro daily.
I appeal 'here to the minister to look into this matter thoroughly and 'endeavour to have the difficulty straightened out. Just the other day I received, as I am sure my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Langworthy) did also, a resolution passed by the Port Arthur Chamber of Commerce, and in the past I have received various other resolutions along the same line advocating this change. It is possible there may be some slight damage done to the Canadian National Railways, which have a line to Duluth, but it is such a roundabout line that it is rot fair to ask 14011-102i
anybody to use that line unless he has no other way of going. The Canadian National Railway runs a service only three days a week to Duluth, and one has to leave at four in the afternoon and does not get into Duluth until eight o'clock next morning, changing at Fort Frances at two in the morning. The _ bus service is much more convenient, leaving at nine or ten in the morning and getting into Duluth at five or six in the afternoon, after 'a very pleasant trip along the lake shore, which by the way is one of the most beautiful automobile drives on the American continent. Last year over 5,000 American cars crossed the bridge at the international boundary and entered1 the Dominion, and this traffic is increasing very rapidly every year. I again urge the minister to look into this matter thoroughly and endeavour to straighten out this ridiculous law; or regulation which prevents the use of these bus lines by citizens of Fort William and Port Arthur and by the people in the sum unding farming country.

Just a word in answer to
my hon. friend. I received his letter this morning, and I have already given instructions to the officers in my department to investigate and see if something cannot be done to meet his wishes. The great difficulty in connection with that bus line is the fact that they are using American busses that have not paid duty, and if we met my hon. friend's wishes we would be allowing American manufacturers to use in Canada American busses for commercial purposes without duty having been paid upon the value of the bus. There should, I think, be a provision in the law by which part of the duty might be collected in a case of this kind, but I fear that to open the door and give this particular bus line the permission requested by my hon. friend would be creating a precedent that might work havoc perhaps to many Canadian lines operating in other parts of Canada. However, I will look into the matter, and if it is possible to do so, my hon. friend's wishes will be met.

I had never heard before the argument my hon. friend has just made, but even if it is as he states, and I accept his word at once, I would point out that there is no other bus line in competition in this case. I do not think there would be enough local traffic on the Canadian side of the line to permit this bus line to pay any part of the duty, because a large proportion of the farmers in the surrounding country and of the citizens of Fort William and Port Arthur have cars of their

own, and only a very small proportion would use this bus line. I think a temporary ruling might well be made to permit this bus line to carry local traffic until such time as a Canadian bus line is established.

Yes, that is it.
I am told by my deputy minister that that is the amount reimbursed to us by the railway companies.

I understand that, but the point I am making is that it is too small an amount, in view of the hon. minister's statements as to a million and a half this year, or when reduced, as he later states, to $769,000, whereas last year it was only $400,000 altogether.

There is certainly some other item or account under which refunds of salaries and other amounts paid back to the department are accounted for. I shall get the information and give it to my hon. friend tomorrow if possible.
And the minister will be * good enough to indicate the amount for the year 1924-25.

If the matter is just left in the Way my hon. friend puts it, it appears to me that perhaps fairness is not being done to his department. This is looked upon as a matter of revenue purely and simply. It is something that is not taken into consideration when arriving at the figures showing the co^t of collection. I admit it is merely a summary and he can only give a rough estimate, but if he is right in his idea that there is perhaps a million and a half of salaries altogether repaid to his department, and if that merely comes in as revenue instead of as reduction of the cost of running the department, it is manifest that the department is not getting credit for nearly the service given to the country and the ratio of cost. I should think the subject would be well worth looking into.

My hon. friend is perfectly right. I am informed that in previous years the department was authorized to credit to its expenses the refunds made to it for salaries. The vote that was formerly asked for was in reality the net amount of the vote actually expended by the department for the collection of revenue. Under instructions from the Auditor General the new system has been adopted. Now every dollar expended must be voted by parliament, and the refunds made must be credited to revenue.

The auditor may be right for the purpose of bookkeeping in connection with the matter of salaries themselves, but if it is done in the department that way, as a matter of fairness to the officers of the department I should have thought the items coming in would have been applied in connection with salary lists, and that the general public would not have been given credit for those items as they are when it comes in as casual revenue. That may have something to do with the matter. It may be my hon. friend's accounts this year have been unusually swollen by reason of that fact. I was looking back at the vote of 1921-22, when we were told we were horribly extravagant in connection with the administration of this department.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "hear, hear." I am afraid he must of necessity vote against this item, because we were told we were extravagant in connection with this very vote of salaries and contingent expenses in the different ports of the Dominion, and the vote then was $1,234,000 less than the public are asked to pay this year. It may well be that the new ruling of the Auditor General accounts for something of that.
It accounts for about
I would have thought my hon. friend has rather in his opening taken away from himself that defence, because he pointed out that the increases-
For last year.

-for last year were very small, but perhaps it might have come in the year before, when there was about half a million of an increase. It may be that that was when the direction of the Auditor General was putting the department in an unfortunate position. It is the sort of thing we should know about at once, because on the face of it, it now looks as if the public were being asked to pay for the same services much more money than they ought to pay, particularly when the government are so fond of telling us that they are reducing the cost of living, the cost of the public services and the like, so that the dollar to them is worth far more than it was in 1921. If I were to adopt just what these hon. gentlemen say themselves, their extravagance on the face of it is perfectly appalling in connection with this item, because not only is the vote swollen by $1,234,000, but the dollar is worth so much more. My hon. friend will remember that when we started discussing this item he was able to show

economy because older men had been retired and new men had been appointed. My hon. friend shakes his head. I think he will find that is what he pointed out. I think he will find that he stated in connection with these additions to the staff that forty-eight men were appointed at a cost of $59,210 and that by reason of retirements and the like there was economy in other directions, the net increase being thereby reduced. If I am wrong in that I want to be put right at once, but that is my recollection of what he said.

I will correct my hon. friend. I said that the net additions to the staff accounted for an increase of $59,210. Decrease due to promotions, appointments and retirements filled by lower paid men, amounted to $57,330. There was also a statutory increase of $169,530.

Mr. Chairman, before
recess the Minister of Customs and Excise was good enough to intimate that he would supply particulars of the amount which will 
be refunded to the department in respect to Sunday work and so on performed by his officials for the accommodation of certain companies. He suggested at first that the amount would be probably a million and a half, but subsequently he made it $700,000 odd. However, I did not understand him to say that he could furnish particulars; I should judge that the amount must be at best an estimate. I call his attention to the fact that the same item apparently occurred in 1924-25, and that the only amount in the Auditor General's statement of revenue that would appear to cover such transactions is an item of $400,000 under casual revenue. The minister is to get those figures to show how the estimate for the present year is made up.
I call my hon. friend's attention to the first page of the Auditor General's report where reference is made to the custom that has existed for some time of the retention of certain moneys by the department to pay drawbacks, and so on, from revenue. The amount of such moneys in 1924-25 was $22,500,000-I am giving round figures. The Auditor General says that the general summary of revenue does not include this item of $22,500,000-
-which, though included in the revenue deposits to the credit of the Receiver General in the first instance, was subsequently refunded as drawbacks of Customs, Excise refunds and similar items chargeable to revenue.
The minister states that no refunds of wages are included in that $22,500,000. The Auditor General says this retention is-
-in accordance with a long standing custom. This custom has been brought to the attention of the House of Commons in previous reports.
May I ask the hon. minister whether he has considered it a desirable state of affairs that $22,500,000 should be received and credited to the Receiver General and disbursed by the Department of Customs and Excise, but not through the ordinary course of vouchers, checked and approved by the Auditor General ? It just occurs to one that when there is a sum of $22,000,000 odd available by the department to pay drawbacks and' refunds, it would be well that that sum should pass through the ordinary system of accounting by the Auditor General. I do not suggest anything wrong at the moment, but it does provide a fruitful field for favouritism and that sort of thing in the refunding of moneys, unless we have a close check and a properly audited voucher system for that amount.
Then I draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that the figures he gave me for 1924 and 1925, receipts $249,000,000, disbursements $7,700,000-again I am using round

Supply-Customs
figures-which show the percentage of cost to revenue as 3.08 per cent, cannot be made up by a reference to the Auditor General's summary on page 30, part D, volume II of his report. I judge that in that amount one will find $22,000,000, the sum which I have referred to just now. If that is so, I would point out that 122,000,000 should not be credited to revenue there because it is to be paid out again, and if it is taken off the figures which my hon. friend has given, his percentage of cost to revenue suffers a slight increase. If I am right in my contention that result follows. The point of my remarks is simply that my hon. friend may be doing himself an injustice in charging as salary an amount which includes payments which are to be returned. On the other hand I should like again to draw his attention to the point raised by the Auditor General, referring to the custom of disbursing $22,000,000 otherwise than through the ordinary channel. My last point is the combination of the previous two, in the statement showing the percentage which he gave me. I hope I have made myself clear.

The hon. member has made himself quite clear. The first knowledge I had of this contention on the part of the Auditor General was when I saw the report to which my hon. friend has referred. The matter will be taken up with the Auditor General and discussed with him. I think it will be a very difficult matter to have the Auditor General initial and approve all the vouchers for cheques for refunds. We have a drawback staff which has to go to the factories of the different firms claiming drawbacks, and it is only there that, the actual amount of merchandise imported from other countries and used for export can be determined. All the payments are made from the department here after the drawback claims have been received and checked over by our officials. Whether or not it would be feasible to have a further check by the Auditor General, and whether or not it could be done rapidly enough to not interfere with trade and commerce is a matter that I will not say is under consideration but that I will take under consideration at once.
I think he is quite right about the disparity between the net revenue shown in the Auditor General's report and the gross revenue given by me to the committee this afternoon. The gross revenue of $249,786,807.83 shows the percentage of cost of collection to be 3.08. That is not the percentage of cost of collection to net revenue, but those figures show the actual cost of collection of the revenue. I realize that my hon. friend is perhaps more correct, than I am if it is desired to show the exact cost of collection of net revenue.

Before passing
this item I would like to draw my hon. friend's attention to one matter which we have not yet covered, in connection with the retirements, the amount of pensions which we are paying to men who have been retired, the amount of bonuses and the like. That, in one sense, no longer appears as a cost in connection with this department, but it nevertheless is a cost in connection with the staff of the department. I would like to ask my hon. friend about that now.

I could get a list showing
the retirements, if that is what my hon. friend desires. I want to thank my hon. friend for the point he made in my favour just before adjournment. I agree with him and I thank him for his remark that it is perhaps a little unfair under the system now employed by the Auditor General to make us show as expense moneys paid out in salaries which are eventually refunded to us by other parties.

Certainly there is some change to be made in one direction or the other. Surely the logical thing is to show that not as actual revenue but as something which is going to decrease the cost of the department.

Mr. Chairman, before the item carries I would like to refer again to the question of preventive officers, which was discussed to some extent this afternoon. I might say that around the coast of Prince Edward Island the preventive officers would have to be very numerous to be of any value. I suggest to the minister that a better way, indeed the only way to get results with a coastline such as that of Prince Edward Island, would be to prevent the stuff from leaving the ships. The vessels lie a few miles off the coast, which contains innumerable bays and creeks and rivers and inlets, and in order to prevent material being landed you would have to have preventive officers everywhere. The practice has been, as I understand it, to look after it to some extent by one patrol boat, but it is utterly impossible for one small boat to look after such a coastline. The result is that the traffic is in and out all the time, with perhaps three or four or five vessels close to the coast all summer. It has created a very bad condition there; liquor is very cheap at the vessel, and four or five fellows put up a few dollars each, send out a motor boat and get a case of liquor. That sort of traffic is very heavy, and we have as well the bootleg traffic. Taking all things into consideration I do not see how the Customs department can have any success
Supply-Customs

whatever in stopping the landing of that liquor unless further patrol boats are put on. I do not think enough preventive officers can be put around the coast to prevent it from coming in, and I would like to suggest to the minister that one patrol boat is certainly not sufficient.

At the present time we have in Prince Edward Island two boats, the Margaret and the Buzz. Two boats are not sufficient. It is impossible to place a preventive officer on every creek and inlet on the shores of that island. It is our intention to provide protection' there by more patrol boats. I will not say they will be purchased; it may be that they will be leased, if good boats can be found for the purpose of trying out the system, without entailing too large a capital expenditure.
In regard to offices rented in the customs building in various places, are rentals allowed by the Public Works department, for example, to the Customs department for the use of these offices?
There is no charge made by the Public Works department to the Customs department for these offices.
The buildings are in charge of the Public Works department? It is the other way?

There is no charge either
way.

Item agreed to.
Salaries and travelling expenses of inspectors of ports and of other officers on inspection, preventive service, and in connection with the Board of Customs; the latter including salaries of $1,500 for the chairman, $1,000 each for three memlbers and $500 for the secretary, $854,065.

Why the increase in this
item?

My hon. friend will notice
the increase is very small as compared with the increase in the previous item. This increase is due entirely to what is known under the Civil Service Act as the statutory increases.
I can give the exact number of officers promoted, if my hon. friend insists.

No, but I find myself
wondering sometimes why it is that year after year ever since I have been here, and I have been here nearly ten years now, we get the same story to explain these increases- statutory increases. Do the statutory increases go on indefinitely? That is what puzzles me at times. Suppose we should last another hundred years; will these keep on increasing year after year?

I hope the Civil Service
Commission will be dead by that time.

I hope this government at least may be dead by that time, because I rather think that a lot of these increases are due to this government, and not to the Civil Service Commission at all. It is simply a case of passing the buck to the commission, I am afraid. Would the minister explain whether these statutory increases are going on for all eternity?

I will do my very best. I
will say at once that I had been just as much puzzled as my hon. friend ever since I came here until the matter was explained to me the other day. I do not know whether I shall be able to make myself clear to my hon. friend because the man who explained it did not make himself quite clear to me. I am told that on a certain date every employee blanketed into departments by the Civil Service Act and all employees employed after that date, go into the service at a certain minimum salary. That salary is gradually increased over a period of years and finally reaches the maximum salary. Like my hon. friend, I believed that some day we would reach the happy time when, with those at the top retiring from the service and being replaced by others starting at the minimum figure, we could administer the service without further increase. We could arrive at that point and the service would adjust itself in that way, however, only upon two conditions. The number of employees must not be increased, and the salary scale must not be changed. The reason why "statutory increases" is invoked every year to explain increased estimates is that requests are constantly made to the Civil Service Commission for re-classification and increases in minimum and maximum salaries. I know I have not been clear, but I have done the best I could.

I presume the minister has explained it as well as he knows how, but I think I know as much now as I did when he got up; I confess I do not know very much about it now. It is a very difficult thing to explain. If it were not for the fact that I would be afraid of being misunderstood in this city of civil servants, I would be inclined to ask if none of them die, but being in this city I would not ask that, because some of the press might say I was wishing for some of them to die off. It does seem strange, however, that in every department every session there are these same salary increases, and the same explanation.

Supply-C ustoms
Perhaps it will come in handy next year, when we are in power, to offer the same explanation, but I confess I find the explanation rather difficult to believe at times.
I want to assure my hon. friend that the civil servants who are dead will not blame him for his remarks-
I am not afraid of them.
Let me also say that when his party does come into power in the far and distant future, there will be statutory increases in the estimates to explain.
Do they think they ever will get into power?
Not with the help of my hon. friend.
Perhaps they will, when the civil servants are all dead.

The government is so close there now that the minister has the vision splendid. I want to make a comment on one or two interruptions as well as on the words of the minister. In the first place, the practice of attributing everything to the Civil Service Commission-
We are not doing that.

It was not the minister, but the hon. gentleman to his right. I expected the minister to rebuke him, but he remained strangely silent. The Civil Service Commission has as much to do with these statutory increases as they have to do with the sun spots-just as much.
Except that they make the classifications.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is the law.

It is the law, certainly, but the law is not what the minister explained. The law does not compel the government to give any increases whatever. The law simply places within the discretion of the government certain limited increases which they may apply or not apply, and the intention of the law was that the government would apply them as a reward for assiduous service to the public in the capacity in which the civil servant might be. Consequently, the application of these increases is entirely within the discretion of the administration, and they are responsible for each and every one applied. The power is theirs, but I am afraid the increases have become more or less automatic, and I do not know how it is ever going to be anything else if the practice of this government is followed. They have taken a 14011-103
certain group of civil servants and have increased' their salaries by a very large percentage. They first of all adopted one limitation, and when that did not suit them, they put the increase upon another basis, and then when both failed to meet all the cases they wanted to cover, they abandoned all limitations and gave increases to everybody. Having pursued that course, I do not see how the government is in a position to deny almost anything to the civil servants underneath. Consequently, the automatic principle applies, and away goes the statutory increase every time; all limitation is abandoned. But there is no mystery about it all. Nor is there very much hope in the words of the minister when he says that the time may come some time when those who go out at the far door, the large-salaried men, will be so numerous that the amount saved in that way will offset the statutory increases, and that we will thus get to a point where the expenditure for salaries will be stationary. There were just as many old men when this law was enacted as there are to-day. There were just as many men fit to be retired the first day this law went into effect as would be retirable next year, or ten years from next year. Consequently there is no hope that the increased retirements later on will have any more effect in offsetting the statutory increases than those retirements have to-day. The only way it could be offset would be either to abolish the power or to restrict the application of the power by some system of discrimination. I do not really see that it is much good to give statutory increases while they are automatic. If they are to apply to everybody why, of course, they are no incentive to service at all. If everybody is to get them, then service does not make them any more helpful to the man who works than if he did not work at all. He might as well be talking to the girls around the corner as working if he is going to get his statutory increase just the same. What I want to impress on the minister is this: he must take the responsibility for the statutory increases himself; he cannot shift it upon the statute, much less can he shift it upon the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are put into a class and they get the increase automatically until they reach the maximum of that class.

Will the minister read
the statute?

Has there been a reclassification of the civil service every year? The minister rather pointed to that fact, but is there such a reclassification? In the short experience I have had here I have heard of the efforts made by civil servants to get themselves reclassified. They are naturally ambitious to get into a higher classification, and I have no doubt that constant effort is being made by various civil servants to attain that end. Now, has it become the practice under this government to 'have a reclassification every year, and does that account for the increase?

No. There has been no
general classification since the government came into power, but there are partial reclassifications every year. The most frequent reclassification is a reclassification increasing the minimum and maximum salary of a certain class of employees.

effect in raising this item?

No, and I agree with what
my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition has said concerning the right of the government to refuse to give the statutory increase to the employees.
Hear, hear.

The government is empowered to do that, but the government led by my right hon. friend did not refuse to do it. I am very sure my right hon. friend did not say he would refuse to do it when he spoke at the Auditorium on the eve of the last election.

I did not refer to the
subject at the Auditorium, save to correct just a few foolish rumours circulated by the friends of the minister. But I am aware, distinctly aware, that in eases we did refuse the statutory increase, and that I did myself, so that the minister will have another apology coming in addition to that of this afternoon

In my department, when
the inspector makes a report that an officer's conduct is only fair, no statutory increase is given to him, but where his conduct and efficiency is better than fair he is given his statutory increase.

Perhaps my
hon. friend, since we are getting into this kind of experience-trying to find out what the other fellow did, and matters of that kind -would turn his attention to another direction and explain why it is, if things were done so loosely under the former administration, with no refusals to increase here, there, and everywhere, he has got to ask for $232,000 more for his department than was asked under the former administration? That would be very much to the point if he would do it.

I do not accuse the last
government of such terrible looseness, I said that the last government-and I am not blaming them for it-gave the statutory increases to all employees who were worthy of them. We have been doing the same thing. But my right hon. friend is certainly not referring to the proper item, because the total increase in this item is only $40,816.
That is since last year.
I am taking my hon. friend back to the time when, as he says, the former administration did not stop increases. I am going back to the year 1921-22.
That is too far.
To 1921-22, four years ago, is that too far? It is the last year to which we can go.

That is not too far but my
hon. friend will admit that at that time the bonuses paid to the civil servants were voted separately and did not form part of the item that the hon. member brings into comparison with this vote.

There was a
bonus, there is no question about that; but the bonus falls very far short of making up this increase, which roughly speaking, is something like 40 per cent in this vote. Now as

to the vote asked by the Conservative administration, I am taking the year I have mentioned, but I could go farther back and get a lower amount; I could go back to 1921, which was our last complete year. But I am not doing that; I am taking a year in which this government had to do with three months of the preparation of the costs, a year in which they submitted estimates which they claimed were our estimates. I can make the position much worse if I take 1921, but I do not do that; I am minimizing the situation as much as I can, and I find that under this vote all that was asked in 1921-22 was $621,380, whereas to-day we are asked to p.ay $854,055. There is an increase of $232,675 on an item of $600,000 odd. Perhaps it would be much better if my hon. friend, instead of going into ancient history, would explain why it is we have an increase of that kind in the period of four years.

I want to assure my hon.
friend that I do not want to go into ancient history; I would be perfectly satisfied to explain the increase for the present year.
My hon. friend cannot take it coming and going, just when it suits him to take it. I am quite sure he would be quite content to take all the estimates without any explanation at all.
Oh, no.

I would not
blame him in tin slightest for being so content. But, Mr. Chairman, here we have an increase during the lifetime of this government-I have not figured it out, but it must be 40 per cent- in a mere matter of administration and that applies to a government Which is making all kinds of extravagant claims to economy. Now the best way to test this claim is to test it right in connection with this particular vote we have before us. What excuse is there for this "government of economy" increasing that vote 40 per cent? It is not a matter of ancient history, but I am trying to see where we are going to wind up. Has my hon. friend reconstituted his board of customs?
No we still have the same board.
Are there any new jobs in the board of customs?

Messrs. Farrow, Blair,
Breadner, Taylor and Wilson are still the members of the board.	[DOT]
If there is no increase in the number, why is the vote changed? Why is the $1,500 put in?

There is $1,500 which is paid to the chairman of the board. If my right hon. friend will refer a few years back he will find this same vote in the estimates of previous years. It was taken out when the salaries of the deputy ministers was raised to $8,000.
Will the minister show where it ever was in?
It was in before. I have not the estimates for former years at hand.
I cannot see it.

When the deputy minister was receiving a salary of $6,000 he was given an allowance of $1,500, as chairman of the board of customs. When the salary was raised to $S,000 that $1,500 was withheld, but the allowance made to the other members of the board was still paid. Mr. Breadner does not receive any salary as a member of the board of customs but his salary is $10,000. The other members of the board of customs receive $1,000 allowance as members of the board and the chairman receives $1,500.
So that he gets $9,500?
He will get that amount if this item is passed.
I thought it was an increase, and ventured to say so, but the minister's first words intimated that it was the same as it always was.
I did not mean to do so.

It is an increase of $1,500 -from $8,000 to $9,500. Last year this item was out. I have the estimates of previous years before me, but not the whole of them, I have last year's estimates and I do not see such figures at all. The item reads:
Salaries and travelling expenses of inspectors of ports and of other officers on inspection, preventive service, and in connection with the board of customs.
The details are not given, but at any rate this is an increase over last year of $1,500 for one official. It all indicates the process by which the quarter million was arrived at in the three years.
Do I understand the chairman of the board of customs receives $9,500?

The deputy minister of the department is at the same time chairman of the board of customs. If my hon. friend will look at the salaries paid the deputy ministers of the different departments he will find several of them receive a salary of $10,000 a year. Some receive $8,000 and some $6,000, depending upon their years of service. The
Supply-Customs

number of years of service of the present deputy minister should qualify him for the higher amount. The commissioner of taxation, the deputy minister of finance, and the deputy minister of justice are receiving $10,000 or more. Having seen my deputy at work and appreciating his devotion and ability, I thought it only fair to give him the same salary or very nearly the same salary as the other deputies were receiving.
I was going to ask about how long the minister expected that it would take to get all of the others up to this amount?
Some of them are above that now.
I know, the process is on.

No, the process will depend on the years of service, and perhaps some of those there now, under the system referred to by my right hon. friend, will have retired before the others advance. We hope some day under this regime,-and perhaps later on under the regime of my right hon. friend, that we will reach that point where there will never be any more statutory increases, where every public servant will be perfectly satisfied with his position, where everybody will be completely remunerated, and everybody will be perfectly happy.

It would be the last thought in my mind to say a word against my hon. friend the deputy minister of customs, for whom I have the utmost respect. I have had dealings with him in an official way, and have every respect for him; this is not a personal reference to him. But I do say that a salary of $8,000 a year for a deputy minister, unless for some special cause, would appear to me, where it is a life job, as a deputy minister's job is, to be a pretty fair salary. Lawyers, doctors or other professional men- and most of them, with the rare exceptions of the very outstanding men in the profession, have at least as great a training as a deputy minister would have-would be quite satisfied with a life annuity of $8,000 a year. I notice that whenever there are any positions open, even if the salaries are about $4,000 a year many lawyers, doctors and other professional and business men are quite ready to apply for them. I do not believe in being niggardly in regard to salaries paid to public officials. I believe we should pay men from whom we get good work a reasonable salary. At the same time I repeat that $8,000 a year, generally speaking, without some special cause, should be a pretty reasonable salary for a

I put it at this figure because the minister practically asserted again and again this evening, that he could cut out probably much more than that, but he could cut out that much without embarrassing the department at all.
Amendment (Mr. Manion) negatived.

Now that the House has satisfactorily swallowed the protestation of the minister, and he has practically swallowed himself, I may point out that he has told us one thing I was not sure about before. We are told that we are now on preventive service, and I would ask the minister whether any of the salaries here covered are salaries of officials who are at present under suspicion or suspension.

No, the salary of any official who is at present under suspicion or suspension is covered under the second item on the next page, which reads:
To provide for expenses of maintenance of revenue cruisers and for preventive service.
The present item merely covers the preventive service staff here and the inspection officers.
Are any of the people who come under this item covered by the Duncan report?

No. Some of those mentioned in the Duncan report are paid out of the first item passed this evening, and others mentioned in the same report are also paid out of the second item on page 62. Those are regular preventive service men.

Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous-Printing and stationery, subscriptions commercial papers, flags, dating stamps, locks, instruments, etc., for various ports of entry, express charges on samples, stationery and legal forms, legal expenses, premiums on guarantee bonds, and uniforms for Customs officers, $480,000.
We are very proud, Mr. Chairman, to see you where you are, but I am going to give you a little word of advice at the start; you will have to speak a little louder. *

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I shall be very glad to oblige my hon. friend.

Could the minister explain why there is an increase of $25,000? He cannot explain it on the ground of statutory increases.

Supply-Customs

The best explanation is that we tried to meet my hon. friend's request two or three years ago and we cut $100,000 off this item. We found that we had cut off too much, and we are obliged to ask that one-quarter of that amount be added to the vote for this year.

What was the
expenditure last year?

I have here the chief accountant's memorandum on this particular item, which reads:
The expenditure for the first six months of 1924-5 was $201,920.31. Proportionately for the entire year the expenditure should have been approximately $404,000, whereas it actually amounted to $455,502.28, a difference of $51,500.
For the first six months of 1925-6 the expenditure was $227,097.44, which proportionately would be $454,000 for the entire fiscal year, which is approximately the total expenditure of the previous year.
The increase for the six months 1925-6 over 1924-5 is $25,177.13, which is accounted for by payment in 1925-6 of guarantee bond premiums, covering the last half of 1924-5, $10,090, for which similar payment did not occur in 1924-5; and payment of printing and stationery accounts of 1924-5, $21,145, which did not occur in the previous year. These two amounts total $31,235 increase, which is reduced to the difference of $25,177.13, being lesser general expenditure during the year 1925-6.

The description of the item would indicate that a good deal of the money was spent on office supplies, guarantee bond premiums and uniforms. Would the minister divide the sum into major items? We do not want the smaller items; but give us a general idea of how it is spent.

The largest amount generally expended under this vote is that paid to the Canadian Bank Note Company of Ottawa for excise stamps. The amount paid for the printing and excise stamps is approximately $165,000 per year. That is one of the largest amounts. All the forms used in the service are printed by the Department of Printing and Stationery, but they are charged to the Department of Cuslums anu cost over $100,000 per year. At all the ports where rve have officials in railway stations, on trains and at points of vantage, they are uniformed. The uniforms are purchased by the officers themselves, but they are paid for by the government in the form of an allowance of $37.50 per annum. A uniform is supposed to last for two years. This item amounts to $58,961.50. Freight and express charges amount to approximately $17,000 and guarantee bond premiums, $8,000. The other amounts are very small.
What about legal expenses?

The legal expenses are not
large. There are certain court costs in connection with actions taken by the department. If my hon. friend will look up the Auditor General's report, part D, page 126, he will see the expenditure in connection with a similar vote for the year 1924-25 when legal expenses amounted to only $245.

I think when
the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) asked the minister as to the reason for the increase and pointed out that it could not be a statutory increase, the minister said that was quite true; there were no statutory increases, but the trouble was that he had tried to do what the hon. member wanted him to do, namely, to economize and that there had been a cut of $100,000 in the vote. Am I right in so understanding the minister? Because I am afraid he will have to fall back on the old statutory increase; there was no cut in the vote last year.

If my hon. friend desires
to say that the vote last year is the same as the vote this year, he is right. What I said was that the amount estimated for this item for 1924-25 was reduced by $100,000 over that of the previous fiscal year, 1923-24, and we reduced it too much. Since that time we have been trying to get along but we find that it is absolutely impossible to meet expenses without increasing the vote. We are not puting it back to the figure at which it stood before; we are increasing it by nearly $25,000.
My hon. friend certainly gave me the impression that he had made a cut last year; that he had tried to cut of! $100,000-

I have not yet been given
an opportunity to make any reductions.

-and therefore there had to be an increase this time. There certainly was not a reduction under the vote of the year before. In 1921-22 I find it was the same old story. The vote in 1921-22 instead of being larger is smaller; it was only $423,000 while the vote to-day is $480,000.

What was the vote in
1923-24?

I have just the vote for 1921-22. I keep to that year because it was the year so often talked about in the country by my hon. friend and those with him as the year of the high water mark of extravagance from which my hon. friends were to work down. I find instead, however, that
Supply-Customs

they are always working up. The vote under this head in 1921-22 was $423,000. My hon. friend must get some other excuse. I think he will have to get a third one.

I told my hon. friend that in 1924-5 this vote had been reduced by $100,000 from that of the year 1923-24. Since that time it has not been increased and we find that we must increase it in order to prevent asking for supplementary estimates every year. I am glad my hon. friend pointed out that even to-day it is only
10 p.m. $55,000 larger than it was in 1921-22, because that is the admission he has just made. At that time we did not have, as we have now in the Department of Customs, the collection of the sales tax and all the other added forms of taxation. We had not started the inspection of all firms owing sales tax, and as my hon. friend knows, the sales tax is not even yet entirely collected on every line of business. It was not all collected by my hon. friend and his government. My officers are tracing people every day who are not paying and who should pay sales tax. That means all kinds of expenditure, and so when my hon. friend says that the item is only $55,000 more than it was in 1921-22, I think he is paying us quite a compliment.
My hon. friend is extremely ingenious, but the trouble with him is that he always forgets the facts.
He is always ready to stand corrected.

I hope my h.on. friend will be a little more careful with the facts. The sales tax was in operation for two years at that time and moreover it was being collected on far more articles than is the case to-day. My hon. friend knows that or certainly he ought to know it.
It was not all collected.

It is not all
collected now. The minister is not collecting anything more by reason of the increase under this particular item. He knows that in connection with his sales tax where he gets anything more is through his travelling auditors. But I do not care which item that comes under; the point is that there was a larger field of work to be done in connection with the sales tax in that year than there is today.
But it was not done.

My hon. friend may say that it was not done, but it was done fairly well and if we look at the arrears which we have had under this government in connection with the sales tax, we shall have a job to find anything much worse done- favoured people here and favoured people there, suits here and no suits there. All rnj' hon. friend has to do is to go through the returns I had made two years ago in this House to know the absolute truth of what I am saying. The fact is that the vote was less then. I have been trying to find the year to which my hon. friend refers.
That is 1923-24.

Perhaps my
hon. friend has it.

I am sorry to say I have
not. I have a statement by the chief accountant which I can read to my hon. friend. I may have been misled.
My hon. friend is right. His government did put on $100,000 for the sake of taking it off afterwards.

: What boats, if any, have we doing similar work on any of the Great Lakes?
We have none.

Is there any
patrolling of exports from Belle River and adjacent places?
No, they are not patrolled.
:	Are they patrolled in any other way?

Yes they are carefully
watched and an export entry is taken for every shipment of goods received, with the name of the boat and a description of the cargo. That information is given to an American officer in accordance with the terms of the treaty with the United States concerning smuggling.
Since when?

Since about September, 1925, when regulations were made under the treaty. Some slight changes have been made in the instructions issued to the officers since the regulations were put into force. We have endeavoured to prevent export entries to Mexico or Cuba when the liquors were to be loaded at a lake port. These export entries were never accepted, but were replaced by new export entries prepared and signed by a duly authorized agent of the shipper at the port. My deputy has now issued instructions that the export entry or entries showing the United States to be the ultimate destination of the goods must accompany each shipment from the time it leaves the distillery in Canada.

When was that regulation
made?
If my hon. friend is referring to the regulation forbidding the exchange of export entries, it was issued on February 13.

Are there no regulations
as to the size or the kind of boats by which these shipments must be consigned?

No. The only clause in
the treaty is that we shall not allow shipment of any kind of liquor from a lake port on a boat which cannot reach the destination to which it is cleared.

Is there any patrol
preventive service on the Pacific coast?

On the Pacific coast we have a rented cruiser which is operated by the department in the same manner as our patrol boats on the Atlantic. There have been complaints of smuggling in British Columbia, and I think the service will have to be improved fhere by the addition of other patrol boats.

Why do you not use the
Canadian Merchant Marine for that purpose?
Mr. BOIVIN.: Those boats are too large.
How many seizures have been made on the Atlantic?

Some of our boats have been very successful. The Margaret, for instance, has made several seizures, and several of the other patrol boats have reported infractions of the law to preventive officers on shore and thus enabled them to make seizures. I am frank to admit, as I have already done to-day, that the preventive service is not what it should be. I am not getting the results that we would like to get from it. I hope by closer co-operation with the provincial authorities to do much better.

Can the minister give
the committee any idea of the number of seizures?

The number of seizures of
liquor smuggled in from the ocean to the Maritime provinces during the open season last year was about forty. There should have been a great many more.

There is one question I would like to ask the minister. If I understand these estimates correctly, in the two columns it just shows the estimates for the fiscal year. Is it not possible to have another column showing the amounts spent during the last fiscal year?

In making up the estimates we have followed the usual custom, and the amount expended during the last fiscal year has never appeared. My hon. friend will find, however, that the expenditures detailed in the Auditor General's report correspond exactly with the votes in the estimates for the previous year. He can find in the Auditor General's report under the same number a description of the expenditures made under eadh item voted last year.

My hon. friend 'has made the same slip several times before. A person trying to follow the books would be hopelessly lost if he followed my hon. friend's directions. I have not. That would

W'hat I am willing to offer my hon. friend is this: I will get a complete list of these ports which should be watched by preventive officers, and I will not ask to go any further to-night. After we have passed this item of $376,510, we shall let the remainder stand for further discussion. I will have the list of outports to-morrow.

I take it the
suggestion is that we stop business now?

then take up another department.

I see no reason
why we should drop this and go to something else. We allowed the government to take up estimates to-day without a motion, and I see no reason why the government should now call some other estimates, just for the purpose of obviating a motion. That can be the only reason.
